newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Angola war foes to form unity government - U.N.
newsitem.headline: Angola war foes to form unity government - U.N.

text.p: Angola's war rivals will form a government of national reconciliation on January 23 in a landmark move on the country's path to peace after nearly two decades of civil war, the United Nations said on Friday.
In a further move towards peace, nine generals of the opposition UNITA movement were inducted into the Angolan Armed Forces (FAA) on Friday.
Earlier on Friday, the U.N. Angola Verification Mission (UNAVEM) in Luanda laid out a detailed timetable for steps towards formation of the unity government in a statement sent to Johannesburg.

It said the dates, agreed on Thursday by the government of President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and the opposition UNITA (National Union for the Total Indedependence of Angola), "mark the beginning of a new chapter in the Angolan peace process".
"The Angolan government of unity and national reconciliation will assume its functions on January 25 following its formation two days earlier," the statement said.
"Other key dates include the return of UNITA deputies to Luanda on January 10 and their assumption of responsiblities in the national assembly on January 17."
The statement quoted Alioune Blondin Beye, special U.N. envoy to Angola, as saying:
"We have taken giant and decisive steps... This good news is a New Year's present to the Angolan people from their leaders."
South Africa said in a separate statement it was encouraging that the unity government would be in place next year.
The Department of Foreign Affairs said South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki held fruitful talks with Angolan officials on a visit to the country this week.

"It was encouraging to learn that the peace process had progressed to such an extent that a government of national unity and reconciliation is expected to be in place as early as next January," the statement said.
The United Nations said in a later statement that the nine UNITA generals were inducted into the Angolan Armed Forces on Friday while other ranks would begin joining the unified army on January 6.
The statement quoted Beye as saying at the swearing in ceremony at army headquarters in Luanda that more and more people were now believing in the Angolan peace process.
"The enemies of peace are dwindling, while the camp of the optimists grows stronger," Beye said.
UNITA and the dos Santos government signed a peace pact in November 1994. About 7,000 UNAVEM peacekeeping troops have been monitoring implementation of the pact's provisions.
The U.N. group said last weekend that some 70,000 rebel soldiers and police had entered 15 demilitarisation camps in the former Portuguese colony.
"UNAVEM considers that UNITA has fulfilled all military tasks required of it," it said.
"All obstacles to completing the formation of the Angolan Armed Forces and the extension of the state administration throughout the national territory have been removed."
